title: What is known about 1RB1RD_1LC0RF_1LD0LB_1RE0RB_---1RA_0LA1RC
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RD_1LC0RF_1LD0LB_1RE0RB_---1RA_0LA1RC.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The tape is a list of levels, each a run of ones 1X followed by 1111110 00 and a run of words (1111110)Y. On the active level each cycle removes one word and adds 15 ones; when the words run out the head rebuilds the ones into a new run of words, about one per 7 ones. Lean proves the machine's basic moves and that it can only halt at the right end of the tape, where the active level works; there a halt needs the head to enter the short last run of ones in the wrong phase (state E with length 2 mod 6, or A with 1 mod 6), which never happened in 217783 steps of an exact accelerated simulator.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (E0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: A halt can only happen past the right end
claims.text: A closed tape language from windows of 4 cells covers the run from blank tape; in it the halting transition E0 can only fire with blank tape from the head on: the machine halts iff E steps onto the blank region right of the tape (after D0 → 1RE on the last cell's neighbour).

claims.title: Four shift rules
claims.text: For every n: C walks left over 1<sup>n</sup>; C walks left through (0111111)<sup>n+1</sup>, shifting every 0 one cell right; the glider 110 (state B) passes a<sup>n</sup> unchanged; E turns 1<sup>7+6n</sup> into words of five ones.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in 2<sup>17783</sup> steps
claims.text: An exact simulator on stacks of words (big integers) with cycle jumps; every jump is first replayed with its changing numbers as variables (affine forms, all comparisons decided for all values) and used only if the replay closes. Checked against a cell-by-cell run at 431,269 macro configurations (2·10<sup>7</sup> steps) and against its plain version at 7,807 sample points up to 10<sup>10</sup> steps. Four minutes: 2<sup>8269</sup> steps (about 10<sup>2489</sup>); 9.5 minutes: 2<sup>17783</sup> steps (about 10<sup>5353</sup>), 180,000 jumps; no halt.

claims.title: The last run decides by its length mod 6
claims.text: When the head enters the last run of ones 1r (blank after it) moving right, it halts iff it is in E with r ≡ 2 (mod 6) or in A with r ≡ 1 (mod 6); otherwise it turns back. Finite check for r ≤ 300, extended to all r for E by ones_to_words. With windows of 7 cells the closed tape language also needs r ≥ 6.

claims.title: The cycle of the active level
claims.text: Every 8 visits of the right end, X + 15 and Y − 1 on the last level, until Y = 0; read off direct runs to 1.2·10<sup>10</sup> steps. The accelerator proves each instance it uses by a symbolic replay (for all values above a base), but the general cycle is not a Lean theorem.

claims.title: Rebuilds at about 7 ones per word
claims.text: When a level is used up the ones are rebuilt into words; sizes grow by about 15/7 per round.

claims.title: Never in the halting phase at the end
claims.text: In all macro configurations of the first 2<sup>38</sup> steps, and of the accelerated run to 2<sup>4025</sup> steps outside its jumps, the head never moves right inside the last run in A with r ≡ 1 or E with r ≡ 2 (mod 6); the last run has at most 15 ones and the head reaches the blank past the end only in state B.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.495).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The level map is not written as one closed formula; a halt needs the head to reach the short last run in state E or A at the wrong length mod 6, which depends on the remainders of the rebuilds.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB0RE_1LC0LE_---1LD_1LE1LB_1RA0LF_0RD1LA up to renaming and mirroring, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. This machine turns ones into seven-cell words and back, level by level, a little like a 3n+1 game with the numbers 15 and 7. This page runs the real machine in your browser and explains the levels.

facts.text: The only place a halt can happen (proved).
Growth of a level per round.
Steps without a halt (exact accelerated simulator, proved jumps).
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.

sections.heading: Levels of ones and seven-cell words
html: Write a for the word 1111110. At step 1.589·109 the tape (right part) reads … 113027 a 00 a2598 130874 a 00 a9 [right end]. Every 8 visits of the right end the last run of words loses one word and the run of ones before it gains 15: 130874 a 00 a9 → 130889 a 00 a8 → … → 131009 a 00.

When the words are gone, the head rebuilds: runs of ones become runs of words, one word for about seven ones, and a deeper level becomes active. At step 9.5·109, for instance, 154794 a 00 a10924 appears. So each round multiplies sizes by about 15/7, and the remainders mod 7 decide how the levels are rebuilt: a Collatz-like system with several counters.

sections.heading: Only at the right edge
html: The machine stops only when E reads a 0, and E is entered only from D reading a 0 (D0 → 1RE). A closed tape language (a finite description, from windows of 4 cells, of every tape the run can produce, checked by Lean's kernel) shows that this can only happen when D stands on the blank cell just past the right end of the tape. Patterns such as a 00 a inside the tape never produce a halt.

The right end is exactly where the active level works (state C visits it every hundred steps or so), so whether the machine stops depends on the state in which the head arrives there after a rebuild: a question about the remainders of the rebuilds, which is open.

sections.heading: The last run of ones, counted mod 6
html: Look at the very end of the tape. It almost always ends with a short run of ones, for instance 11111 0 1111 0 111111111111 (twelve ones at the end). When the head comes from the left and walks right into that last run, what happens depends only on its state and on the length r of the run, counted modulo 6:

Red marks a halt: in state E with r ≡ 2, or in state A with r ≡ 1 (mod 6), the head runs off the end and stops; in all other cases (and in the other four states) it turns back. In every run we could follow, the head always arrived at that last run in a safe phase. So the whole question is whether the rebuilds of the levels, steered by their remainders mod 7, can ever deliver the head to the end in a red phase.

sections.heading: 2<sup>17783</sup> steps without a halt
html: Simulating cell by cell stops being useful after about 1010 steps. The exact simulator in py/ws.py keeps the tape as stacks of runs (this many words of that many ones) and moves through a whole run at once. On top of it, py/cyc.py spots a stretch of the run that repeats with numbers changing by fixed amounts (like X + 15, Y − 1), re-runs that stretch once with the numbers replaced by symbols to prove it works for all larger values, and then jumps over thousands of repetitions in one step.

Checked against the plain machine, this reached 28269 steps (a number with about 2,490 decimal digits) in four minutes and 217783 steps (about 5,350 digits) in under ten, with no halt. That is evidence, not a proof: the machine could still halt later.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

family: nested counters, growth 15/7 (levels of ones and 7-cell words)
summary: Levels 1^X a 00 a^Y (a = 1111110): each cycle X+15, Y-1, then ones are rebuilt into words at about 7 per word (growth 15/7, remainders steer it); Lean proves it can halt only at the right edge, and an exact accelerated simulator with proved cycle jumps ran 2^17783 steps (about 10^5353) without a halt.
